common_name: Ember's Wish Salvia (Salmon-Red Australian Hybrid Sage)

planting.note: Set out nursery starts after frost danger has passed in well-drained, amended beds or large containers; Ember's Wish is an Australian-bred hybrid sage, a sister selection to Wendy's Wish with warm salmon-red flowers.

directions: Give it full sun and good drainage; Ember's Wish tolerates heat and humidity better than many salvias and blooms nearly nonstop through the hot, humid Gulf Coast growing season. A sister selection to the popular Wendy's Wish, it bears warm salmon-red flowers with contrasting dark calyces on sprawling, arching stems, offering a warmer color option within the same vigorous, free-flowering hybrid group prized by hummingbirds and butterflies. Cut back hard in late winter to renew growth, and take softwood cuttings in fall as insurance since plants can be short-lived in wet winter soils. In colder zone 8 pockets treat as a root-hardy perennial and mulch the crown heavily.

common_name: Mysty Salvia (Compact Long-Blooming Blue Mealy-Cup Sage)

planting.note: Set out nursery starts after frost danger has passed in well-drained, amended beds or large containers; Mysty is a compact, sterile mealy-cup sage hybrid that blooms continuously all season without needing deadheading.

directions: Give it full sun and well-drained soil; Mysty tolerates heat and humidity well and flowers continuously from spring through frost. This compact, sterile hybrid between Salvia farinacea and Salvia longispicata produces dense spikes of violet-blue flowers on a tidy, mounded plant that needs no deadheading to keep flowering, since it sets no seed. Its small stature and nonstop bloom make it a strong choice for edging, containers, and mass plantings where taller mealy-cup sage cultivars would be out of scale. Cut back lightly in late winter to renew growth in zones where it persists as a perennial.

common_name: All Gold Lemon Balm (Bright Golden-Yellow Foliage Lemon Balm)

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; All Gold bears bright golden-yellow foliage that holds its color best out of the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; some morning sun deepens the golden foliage color while afternoon shade prevents scorch and leaf burn in hot climates. All Gold bears strikingly bright, uniform golden-yellow leaves rather than the plain green of the species, carrying the same fresh, lemony scent and flavor prized for teas, sachets, and culinary use, and its bright color makes it a strong foliage accent in a partly shaded herb bed even when not being harvested. Cut back hard after flowering to encourage fresh, brightly colored new growth and to reduce self-seeding, since Melissa officinalis can spread aggressively from seed. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

planting.note: Plant rhizome pieces (2-3 inches with at least one bud) 2-4 inches deep after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Hawaiian Red bears showy red-tinged stems and leaf sheaths along with the edible rhizome.

directions: Plant rhizome pieces 2-4 inches deep after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun. Hawaiian Red turmeric bears the same broad, canna-like paddle leaves as standard turmeric, but with striking red-tinged stems and leaf bases that add ornamental appeal to a tropical garden bed even before the pale flower spikes emerge from the leaf bases in summer, all while producing the same aromatic, deep orange-yellow edible rhizome used fresh or dried in cooking. Harvest rhizomes in fall after the leaves die back naturally, which signals the completion of rhizome development, and store a portion frost-free to replant the following spring in zones where the crown does not reliably overwinter. Turmeric grows best under the same warm, humid, partially shaded, consistently moist conditions favored by its ginger relatives.
